title: Fix a Search Tree With Two Swapped Values
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree with distinct values. It used to be valid, but the values of exactly two nodes were swapped by mistake.

Repair it in place by swapping those two values back. Do not change the shape of the tree. The function returns nothing; the tree you were given is checked afterwards.

examples.why: 3 and 8 traded places. In sorted (in-order) reading the tree gives 1, 8, 4, 5, 7, 3, 9: two places where the order drops.
The swapped values are neighbours in sorted order, so the in-order reading 1, 3, 2 drops only once.
The two children traded places; the root was right all along.

hints: An in-order walk of a valid search tree reads the values in increasing order. What does that reading look like after two values are swapped?
The reading has one or two places where a value is bigger than the one after it. The first wrong node is the bigger value at the first drop; the second is the smaller value at the last drop.
Track the previous node during an in-order walk. On the first drop remember prev as first and the current node as second; on a later drop update only second. Swap their values at the end.

explain.intuition:
Read the tree in-order and a valid search tree gives a sorted list. Swapping two values breaks that sorted list in a predictable way. If the two values are far apart, the list has two drops, like 1, 8, 4, 5, 7, 3, 9: the too-big 8 causes the first drop and the too-small 3 causes the second. If they are neighbours in sorted order, there is only one drop, and the two nodes on either side of it are the pair.

So walk in-order while remembering the previous node. At the first drop, record first = prev and second = cur. At any later drop, move second to the new cur. Swap the two values and you are done. The basic walk uses a stack; Morris traversal does the same walk in O(1) extra space by temporarily threading right pointers back to ancestors.
steps: Walk the tree in-order (iteratively, to avoid deep recursion) and keep prev, the previously visited node.
When prev.val > cur.val: if first is empty, set first = prev; in every case set second = cur.
pitfalls: Setting second only on the second drop. When the swapped values are neighbours there is no second drop, and the pair is the two nodes of the first one.
Taking cur at the first drop and prev at the second. The first wrong node is the too-big one, which is prev; the second is the too-small one, which is cur.
Checking each node only against its direct children. A value can be fine next to its parent and still be in the wrong subtree.

complexity.space: O(h) with a stack, O(1) with Morris traversal

solutions.title: Sort the in-order values and write them back
solutions.idea: Collect the nodes in-order, sort their values, and assign the sorted values back in the same order. Correct, but uses O(n) memory and a sort.

solutions.title: In-order walk, find the drops
solutions.idea: Walk in-order with a stack, remembering the previous node. The first drop gives the first wrong node; the last drop gives the second.

solutions.title: Morris traversal
solutions.idea: The same drop detection, but the in-order walk threads each left subtree's rightmost node back to its ancestor instead of using a stack, then removes the thread.

followups: Explain why Morris traversal leaves the tree unchanged when it finishes.
Three values were rotated instead of two swapped. Can you still fix it with one in-order pass?
